Q: How to reduce indentation level of argument help in argparse? A:

Continuing from @wkl's excellent answer:

ArgumentParser takes the formatter_class keyword argument, which expects a class and not an instantiated object. Argparse's formatter classes have the max_help_position kwarg, which is exactly what we want, but because we don't instantiate the class we don't get a chance to set it.

This is exactly the situation partial is for:

import argparse
from functools import partial

partial_formatter = partial(
    argparse.HelpFormatter, 
    max_help_position=10
)

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
    formatter_class=partial_formatter
)

partial returns a callable object that calls the wrapped method but substitutes specific arguments. The object has the same prototype as the wrapped function. It's exactly the right fit here, since we don't want to involve ourselves with argparse's other internals (like tracking prog) with a lambda.

More concisely:

import argparse
from functools import partial

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
    formatter_class=partial(argparse.HelpFormatter, max_help_position=10)
)

So, when this runs, formatter_class gets a method that creates a HelpFormatter, but its max_help_position kwarg will be set to 10 regardless of what ArgumentParser tries to do with it. (Which is to not pass anything and use the default.)

Q: how to get data from the Profile table related to the User table based on user data from the access token in Nest Js A:

Robby,

Seems to me like you are missing a step. The decorator you have made is returning the user object that has been attached to the request. This attachment is made somewhere - likely in a access token strategy that accompanies your access token guard.

In the strategy, you are likely to find a validate method, and this method is likely pulling the user data out of the database. In that very place, you should be joining in the profile data on user.id = profile.user_id or something similar.

If you would show us your validate method, or how you are otherwise populating this user object that is attached to the request we could help you further...

Good luck

Q: Is Websphere written in Java? Does it run so fast in JVM? A:

around 1997, initially was written in plain C and Perl (for the Enterprise Java Bean container EJB1 then EJB2).. NOT in Java and NOT in C++ and NOT in PL/1 and NOT in Smalltalk. Before being commercialized, v1 and v2 run on RS6000 AIX, and one had to customize the Makefile to compile the product... there is a mix up on the original product name.. some confusion (even on Wiki) as some think it was a continuation of IBM failing product "IBM San Francisco" (San-francisco-layers). Well, it is not... finally, the "sphere" names started with an Apple ethernet product for AppleTalk: "INPHOSPHERE", I believe in 1984 or 1985, was also called later on (1992) Liaison, Inphosphere, that was an apple internet router; but there is no trace of it on Google and anywhere else; don't recall if it was a product put by a third party company...

In 1999, IBM acquired some stakes in RedHat, where the green thread (available in kernel 2.2, and short living 1999 to 2000 as Java thread library in Java 1.1), was around that time when IBM started plumbing WebSphere with some Java; things are not that simple, because lot of the code infrastructure is ORB based based (as IBM CORBA, RMI, Distributed Objects was as early as 2000) , the IOR that you can still see today were C based.

In 2002 with WAS v3, after a whole rewrite of the code base, one can see Java, eg. Websphere-3.5-startup-on-IBM-AIX-RS6000

Notice that the JAVA.EXE is an environment variable being set in UNIX AIX startupServer.sh of WebSphere. Note that the .EXE in JAVA.EXE has nothing to do with DOS or NT or PDP or CP/M or even the 1950s punch card to mark the relocatable executable files! The JVMs are cascaded under a process that is bootstrapped: since it is a system program process then it is written in C. Right? We called that the bootstrap process, and underneath it a set of nannies processes are started

Websphere-loading-classes-ring

and here goes the story of WebSphere.. invented it in New York like anything else..

Q: How can users see a list of places they've interacted with under Google Places API Terms of Service? A:

By storing only place_id (and optionally lat/lng for ≤30 days) per user, and calling the Places API when showing the list to get current name/address etc. for display only.

There is a compliant pattern on standard pay-as-you-go.
persist only place_id (and lat/lng ≤30 days); never persist names, addresses, or other Places “content”; use live Place Details requests when displaying the list.
